extracted.intended_audience: actuaries, demographers, mathematicians, and financial mathematicians interested in mortality tables and annuity valuation
extracted.subtask_description: Construct life-tables from city birth/death bills and use them to compute survival odds, insurance prices, and the present value of annuities for one, two, or three lives. Includes practical rules, example tables, and computational shortcuts (logarithms, interpolation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Population suitability for a standard mortality table
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a population where ages and sexes of all deaths are recorded monthly, with minimal influx or efflux of strangers (so the people 'die where they were born'), and where births and funerals are reliably recorded — such a population can serve as a proper standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley selects Breslaw because its bills deliver ages and sexes monthly, the city is far from the sea (few strangers), and births a little exceed funerals. He notes defects in London/Dublin (missing total population, ages not mentioned, large casual accession of strangers) making them unfit as standards. If total population number is lacking it may be estimated by comparison with mortality by age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required data for mortality tables
rubrics_metrics.description: To form dependable mortality tables you need the number of births and funerals and the ages (and sexes) of the people dying, ideally collected monthly over many years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley highlights three defects in existing bills: (1) the total number of people missing; (2) ages of the people dying not recorded; (3) large and casual accession of strangers altering counts. He recommends many years of data (more than 5, preferably ~20) to reduce chance irregularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a life table (numbers living by age)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the bills of mortality derive a table exhibiting the number of persons living at each age from birth to extreme old age; this table shows the chances of mortality and the numbers living of ages current as annexed to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley forms a table giving persons living at each age (e.g., total 34,000 for Breslaw) by using births and deaths by age. This table is the basis for deriving one-year death counts, survival probabilities, and all subsequent annuity calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year survival odds calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The odds that a person of a given age does not die in one year equal the number surviving to the next age divided by the number who die during the year (or expressed as 'remainders' to deaths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: of 567 living at age 25, 7 die in a year, leaving 560 — so the odds a 25-year-old does not die in a year are 560 to 7 (or 80 to 1). Compute yearly survival odds by comparing adjacent age counts in the table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-year survival (odds to attain a given later age)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the odds that a person of one age will live to another age, take the number remaining at the target age and divide it by the difference between that number and the number at the current age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to find odds a man of 40 lives 7 years, take number at 47 (377) and subtract from number at 40 (445) to get deaths (68); odds are 377 to 68 = 54½ to 1. The same method applies for any proposed number of years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Median remaining lifetime ('even lay')
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the age at which there is an even wager (50:50) that a person of a given age will arrive, divide the number living at the given age by two and find the age where the living number reduces to that half.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a person aged 30 has 531 living; half is 265 which falls between ages 57 and 58, so a 30-year-old may reasonably expect to live between 27 and 28 more years (i.e., to ~57–58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for pricing insurance and annuities (single life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purchaser should pay only the proportion of the annuity's value equal to his chance of being alive each year; the value of an annuity equals the yearly sum of the present value of the annual chance of surviving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute for each year: survival probability × present value (discount factor) of one pound payable after that year; sum these yearly present values to obtain the annuity value. Halley gives 'years purchase' values and demonstrates using a 6% interest assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present value discount factors (table for 6% interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decimal present-value multipliers for £1 payable after n years at 6% (e.g., year 1 = 0.9434, year 2 = 0.8900, ... year 100 = 0.0029) are required to convert future contingent payments to present value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley provides a table of decimal present values for 1£ payable after 1,2,... years at 6% and recommends using logarithms to compute present values compactly when tables are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of two lives (joint contingencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: For two lives, multiply the table numbers for each age to obtain the total number of chances; the products of survivors and deceased counts give the probabilities for both alive, both dead, or one surviving the other; use these products in proportions to compute present values for various contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example method: for ages 18 and 35 with numbers 610 and 490, N = 610×490; after 8 years use counts of survivors/deaths (50×73 etc.) to find chances of both dead, one living, etc. Halley illustrates with rectangular parallelogram diagrams to visualize products and proportions. Use product-of-numbers and differences to compute contingent present values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of three lives
rubrics_metrics.description: For three lives multiply the three table numbers; expand the product into eight terms representing every combination of the three being alive/dead (Rrj, r^Y, ... Yyv). Use these products and yearly present values to price annuities contingent on any survivorship condition among the three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley represents these eight products geometrically as a rectangular parallelepiped and shows how to compute reversions (e.g., value of the younger life after the two elders). He demonstrates with a numerical example (lives of 10, 30, 40) and notes that from certain ages only subsets of the lives need be considered as some ages become certainly expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational shortcuts: logarithms and interpolation
rubrics_metrics.description: To alleviate the labor of many multiplications and proportions, use logarithms and do computations at intervals (e.g., every 4th or 5th year) with interpolation for intermediate years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley advises using logarithms to replace repeated multiplications and mentions that instead of computing every single year one may compute every 4th or 5th year and interpolate for the intermediate years. He also describes using complements of logarithms to find present values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation and local adjustment due to salubrity differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality tables derived from one place cannot be universally applied because different places have different salubrity (health conditions); one should prefer a local standard where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley acknowledges Breslaw may not be universal but argues it is a reasonable standard among known places; he urges others to attempt similar compilations for their own cities to allow comparison and better local valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using life tables for demographic and policy uses (e.g., military force estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Life tables can be used to estimate demographic quantities such as the number of persons fit to bear arms by selecting an age range (Halley suggests 18–56 rather than 16–60).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley uses his table to find counts in age ranges and computes that of 34,000 souls, 18,053 fall outside 18–56 and 18,053 inside, estimating the fencible force ~9,000 (half the in-range population assumed male). He suggests this may serve as a general rule for other places.
